text: Introduce yourself and state that you were responsible for the backend part of CODITENT. Explain that the presentation focuses on the system behind the user interface: APIs, data, permissions, asynchronous work, real-time communication, privacy, and deployment. Replace [Your Name] before presenting.
A production-shaped backend with breadth across API design, data, security, asynchronous work, and operations.

Use these numbers as evidence of scope, not as vanity metrics. The repository contains 18 domain routers, 163 route decorators, 29 SQLAlchemy models, 46 Alembic migrations, 53 test files, and 365 test functions at the time this deck was generated. Explain that the important point is the variety of responsibilities: identity, hiring workflows, real-time communication, background jobs, data privacy, and production operations.
The backend connects every recruitment role
CODITENT supports three groups with different data and permissions.
Profiles, CVs, offers, applications, interviews, recommendations and recruiter chat
Offers, candidate review, hiring stages, team invitations, interviews and recruitment chat
Users, companies, invitations, support, institutions, missions and audit activity
I designed and implemented the server-side system that validates requests, enforces access rules, stores data, coordinates workflows, and integrates external services.
The frontend asks. The backend decides what is valid and what each user may do.

Start with the product, not the technology. CODITENT serves candidates, company teams, and platform administrators. Each group sees different resources and can perform different actions. My role was to build the backend boundary that validates requests, protects data, and applies the recruitment rules consistently.
FastAPI controls three paths: immediate requests, durable background work, and real-time communication.
PostgreSQL records and private file storage
Create a durable job or email row
Durable state stays in PostgreSQL. Redis coordinates fast, temporary work. External providers remain behind controlled workers.

Explain the three paths separately. In the request path, Nginx terminates HTTPS and FastAPI validates identity, permissions, and business rules before using PostgreSQL or private storage. In the background path, the API commits durable outbox rows before Redis and Celery coordinate delivery to Gemini or Resend. In the real-time path, a short-lived socket ticket reaches an authorized WebSocket endpoint, PostgreSQL stores message history, and Redis distributes presence and messages across API processes.
A request moves through five layers. Each layer owns one type of responsibility.
Validate transport data and call the next layer
Load the user, session, company, and shared guards
Apply permissions, workflows, and domain rules
Process AI, email, files, and scheduled tasks
Move an application to the interview stage
Routers coordinate the call. Services make the business decision. Database constraints reject invalid state.

Explain the layers from left to right. Routers handle HTTP and WebSocket input. Dependencies load identity and request context. Services make reusable business decisions. Models and transactions protect durable state. Workers handle slow external systems. Use the application-stage example to show the separation in practice: the router validates input, the dependency loads the caller and company, the service checks permission and state transition, and the transaction updates the application while creating notification work.
Async request handling, dependency injection, validation and OpenAPI
Transactions and relational integrity fit recruitment workflows
Async data access with versioned schema changes
Slow AI tasks leave the HTTP request path
Protected CV and image assets with backend-only credentials
Repeatable environments and controlled production deployment
More infrastructure gives better reliability, but it also increases configuration, testing, and operational responsibility.

Explain why each technology exists. FastAPI gives a clear API layer. PostgreSQL protects relationships and multi-step updates. Redis and Celery keep slow AI work away from user requests. Private storage protects CVs. Docker and Ansible make the same architecture reproducible. Mention the cost: each extra component introduces configuration and failure modes that the backend must monitor.
Every request passes through the same security and validation boundary.
Mutating cookie requests require an approved Origin plus a matching CSRF cookie and X-CSRF-Token header.
Expected errors stay explicit; unexpected failures return a safe message and a traceable error ID.

Use one real endpoint as an example. A request first reaches a router, then Pydantic validates its body. Authentication accepts a bearer token or secure access cookie, verifies the JWT, checks session revocation, and loads the current user. Mutating cookie requests also require Origin and double-submit CSRF validation. Authorization checks role, tenant, and ownership. The service applies business rules inside a transaction, and response models prevent accidental data exposure.
The application record connects the candidate, offer, workflow, and conversation.
Foreign keys protect relationships. Unique constraints prevent duplicates. Transactions keep multi-step updates consistent. Alembic versions each schema change.

Center the explanation on the application entity. It connects one candidate to one offer and carries the recruitment stage and CV snapshot. Interviews, chat, screening results, and notifications relate to that workflow. Foreign keys and unique constraints provide a second layer of protection beyond Python code. Alembic makes schema changes explicit and repeatable.
Correctness must survive two users—or two workers—acting at the same time.
Reject updates based on stale state
Example: lock the application, validate its current stage, write the transition and notification work, then commit once.

This slide answers what happens when requests race. Application checks are necessary but not sufficient. Database constraints reject invalid final states. Transactions group related updates. Row locks protect state-machine transitions. Skip-locked claiming lets multiple workers process different jobs without blocking one another. Idempotency keys make retries safe. The application keeps a CV snapshot so later CV edits do not silently rewrite hiring history.
A token identifies a session. Current database state decides whether that session still has authority.
OTP proves control of the address
JWTs carry session ID and auth_version. Redis gives fast rejection; PostgreSQL remains the durable source of truth.
2FA challenges are short-lived and consumed atomically to prevent replay. Trusted devices remain revocable.

Explain the difference between identity and authority. Passwords are hashed with bcrypt and email OTP confirms account ownership. JWTs carry a session ID and authorization version, but protected routes still load current user state. Redis is a fast revocation cache while PostgreSQL remains durable truth, so revoked sessions stay rejected even if Redis is unavailable. Sensitive changes increment auth_version, invalidating old credentials. Two-factor challenges use atomic consumption to prevent replay.
Each protected action combines a permission check with resource scope.
Review, feedback, analytics and stage changes
A member cannot access another organization's candidates or offers
A candidate can access only their own profile, files and applications
Foreign or missing resources return a safe response that avoids leaking private existence.

Authentication answers who the caller is. Authorization answers whether that caller may perform this action on this resource. CODITENT combines a company-role permission matrix with resource scoping. A recruiter may have permission to review applications, but only inside the recruiter’s own company. Candidates remain limited to their own records.
The backend controls every stage change and records the recruitment history.
The service checks the current stage, the requested next stage, the caller's permission, and the application scope before committing the change.

Describe this as a state machine. Users cannot jump freely between stages. The backend checks the current state, validates the requested transition, verifies the caller’s role, and confirms the application belongs to the same company or candidate. The update and related notifications occur consistently inside the workflow.
AI calls can take seconds or fail. The backend keeps them outside the user request.
Transient provider failures do not lose the request

AI powers CV extraction, match context, recommendation ranking, and screening support. Calling Gemini inside the HTTP request would make users wait and could lose work when the API restarts. CODITENT writes durable job state first. Jobs carry a unique dedupe key, retry state, availability time, lease deadline, and lease owner. The dispatcher recovers expired leases; workers heartbeat while processing; the final update checks lease ownership before committing. AI output remains advisory and never replaces authorization rules.
Business changes commit first; email delivery can retry independently without duplicating messages.
Fernet protects the queued email payload
Retries expand from 30 seconds to 60 minutes
Dedupe and provider idempotency make retries safe

Email is a separate reliability problem from the user request. The same transaction that changes the domain state creates an EmailDelivery row, so the intent is durable. The payload is encrypted, and a unique dedupe key prevents duplicate business messages. Workers claim rows with skip-locked row locking, deliver through Resend with a provider idempotency key, and apply bounded retry delays from 30 seconds to one hour.
Real-time delivery stays connected to durable history and recruitment permissions.
A valid login alone is insufficient. The user must belong to the application conversation and the current stage must allow chat.
Workflow events create in-app alerts and durable email work.

Explain that a real-time connection still needs authorization. The client obtains a short-lived socket ticket, then the WebSocket endpoint checks the user and application. PostgreSQL remains the durable source of message history. Redis helps multiple API processes share presence and broadcast messages. Notifications connect stage changes, interviews, and invitations to in-app and email delivery.
CVs and identity data require stricter controls than public offer content.
File type, size, authentication and ownership checks
Backend service credentials access Supabase buckets
The API authorizes access before returning an asset
JSON, CSV, and XML account data
Delete private files and protect workflow integrity
The backend exposes only the minimum data required for the current user and action.

CVs, avatars, and logos do not belong in a public bucket. The backend validates uploads and stores assets privately. Downloads pass through authorization rules. Account controls support export, validated import, scheduled deletion, a cancellation period, file removal, and anonymization of records that must remain for recruitment integrity.
The backend includes the controls needed to run and diagnose the system in production.
Liveness and readiness checks cover required components
Structured events include routes and traceable error IDs
Environment boundaries with Vault support and startup checks
TLS, HSTS, same-origin routing and WAF rules
Docker images, Compose services and Ansible automation
Public traffic reaches Nginx. Database, Redis, workers, and internal service ports remain private.

A backend is complete only when the team can operate it. Health and readiness endpoints distinguish a running process from a usable service. Structured logs and Prometheus metrics help diagnose failures. Nginx handles TLS and public routing. Docker packages the services, while Ansible applies deployment steps consistently. Internal ports stay private.

Tests prove isolated behavior, while the demo proves that the parts work together. During the demo, explain the backend effect of every click. Show authentication, one permission decision, an application record, an asynchronous AI job, and a persisted chat message. Keep database or logs ready so staff can see the server-side result.
What I learned while building the CODITENT backend
A valid token cannot replace role, tenant and ownership checks
Constraints and transactions protect workflows when application code fails
Outboxes and workers protect AI and email jobs from process restarts
Add distributed tracing across API and workers
Improve job retry and failure dashboards

Close with the engineering lessons rather than a feature list. Current database state must drive authorization. Database constraints support application security. Durable queues protect slow external work. Then mention the improvements honestly. Invite questions and be ready to open the code for any component discussed in the deck.
